title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: There are no circumstances a man cannot get used to, especially when he sees everyone around him living the same way. Three months earlier, Levin could not have believed that he would be able to fall calmly asleep in the state he was in that day—living an aimless, irrational life, spending beyond his means, after drinking to excess (he couldn't call what had happened at the club anything else), forming an inappropriately friendly relationship with a man his wife had once been in love with, and paying a still more inappropriate visit to a woman who could only be called a lost woman, after being charmed by that woman and upsetting his wife—he could still drop quietly off to sleep. But under the effect of exhaustion, a sleepless night, and the wine he had drunk, his sleep was sound and untroubled.
At five o'clock the creak of a door opening woke him. He jumped up and looked around. Kitty was not in bed beside him. But there was a light moving behind the screen, and he could hear her footsteps.
"What is it?... what is it?" he said, half-asleep. "Kitty! What is it?"
"Nothing," she said, coming out from behind the screen with a candle in her hand. "I wasn't feeling well," she said, with a particularly sweet and knowing smile.
"What? has it started?" he said in alarm. "We need to send...." and he hurriedly reached for his clothes.
"No, no," she said, smiling and holding his hand. "It's almost certainly nothing. I was just a bit unwell. It's over now."

And climbing back into bed, she blew out the candle, lay down, and was still. Though her stillness struck him as suspicious—as if she were holding her breath—and even more suspicious was the look of peculiar tenderness and excitement she had worn coming out from behind the screen as she said "nothing," he was so sleepy that he dropped off at once. Only later did he remember the stillness of her breathing, and understand everything that must have been happening in her sweet, precious heart while she lay beside him, not moving, awaiting the greatest event in a woman's life. At seven o'clock he was woken by her hand on his shoulder and a gentle whisper. She seemed to be torn between regret at waking him and the wish to talk to him.
"Kostya, don't be frightened. It's all right. But I think.... We ought to send for Lizaveta Petrovna."
The candle was lit again. She was sitting up in bed, holding some knitting she had been working on these last few days.
"Please, don't be frightened, it's all right. I'm not the least bit afraid," she said, seeing his terrified face, and she pressed his hand to her breast, then to her lips.

He jumped up quickly, still barely awake, and kept his eyes fixed on her as he pulled on his dressing gown; then he stopped, still looking at her. He had to go, but he could not tear himself away from her eyes. He thought he loved her face, knew her expression, her eyes, but he had never seen her like this. How hateful and awful he seemed to himself, thinking of the distress he had caused her the day before. Her flushed face, framed by soft curling hair under her night cap, was radiant with joy and courage.

Though there was so little that was complicated or artificial in Kitty's nature in general, Levin was struck by what was now showing through, when suddenly all the layers fell away and the very core of her soul shone out of her eyes. And in this simplicity, this nakedness of her soul, she—the very woman he loved in her—was clearer than ever. She looked at him, smiling; but all at once her brows twitched, she lifted her head, and walking quickly up to him, gripped his hand and pressed close to him, breathing her hot breath against him. She was in pain and was, as it were, complaining to him of her suffering. And for the first moment, out of habit, it seemed to him that he was to blame. But in her eyes there was a tenderness that told him she was nowhere near reproaching him, that she loved him for her suffering. "If not I, who is to blame for it?" he thought without meaning to, looking for someone to hold responsible for this pain so that he could punish them; but there was no one. She was suffering, complaining, and triumphing in her suffering, and rejoicing in it, and loving it. He saw that something sublime was being accomplished in her soul, but what? He could not figure it out. It was beyond him.
"I've sent for Mamma. You go quickly and bring Lizaveta Petrovna ... Kostya!... Nothing, it's passed."
She stepped away from him and rang the bell.
"Right, go now; Pasha's coming. I'm all right."
And Levin saw with astonishment that she had picked up the knitting she had brought in during the night and started working at it again.
As Levin was going out one door, he heard the maidservant come in at the other. He paused at the door and heard Kitty giving the maid precise instructions and starting to help her move the bed.

He dressed, and while they were harnessing his horses—since no cab for hire was in sight yet—he ran back up to the bedroom, not on tiptoe, it seemed to him, but on wings. Two maidservants were carefully moving something in the room.
Kitty was walking about, knitting quickly and giving directions.
"I'm going for the doctor. They've sent for Lizaveta Petrovna, but I'll go on there too. Isn't there anything wanted? Should I stop by Dolly's?"
She looked at him, plainly not hearing what he was saying.
"Yes, yes. Do go," she said quickly, frowning and waving him off with her hand.
He had just stepped into the drawing-room when suddenly a plaintive moan sounded from the bedroom, instantly cut short. He stood still, and for a long while could not take it in.
"Yes, that's her," he said to himself, and clutching his head, he ran downstairs.

"Lord have mercy on us! pardon us! help us!" he repeated, the words coming for some reason suddenly to his lips. And he, an unbeliever, repeated these words not just with his lips. In that instant he knew that all his doubts—even the impossibility of believing through reason, which he was aware of in himself—did not in the least keep him from turning to God. All of that now floated out of his soul like dust. Whom was he to turn to if not to Him in whose hands he felt himself, his soul, and his love?

The horse wasn't ready yet, but feeling an unusual concentration of his physical strength and his mind on what he had to do, he set out on foot without waiting for it, and told Kouzma to catch up with him.

At the corner he met a night cabman driving fast. In the small sledge, wrapped in a velvet cloak, sat Lizaveta Petrovna, a kerchief tied round her head. "Thank God! thank God!" he said, overjoyed to recognize her small, fair face, which wore a peculiarly serious, almost stern expression. Telling the driver not to stop, he ran along beside her.
"Two hours, then? No more?" she asked. "You ought to let Pyotr Dmitrievitch know, but don't hurry him. And get some opium at the chemist's."

"So you think it may go well? Lord have mercy on us and help us!" Levin said, seeing his own horse driving out through the gate. Jumping into the sledge beside Kouzma, he told him to drive to the doctor's.
